Hi all, yesterday I made few more holos, which are better and less milky than last time.

I used the mix 100/12/4 with pH=9 adjusted with TMG and left 24 hours in room temp. There is significant dark reactin, because the plates were qite darker than usually. 

The expose time was cca 20 minutes. 

Processed with the solution of 1000ml H2O; 12,5g pyrosulfate; 5g Alum

Then washed with surfactant, IPA bath 30, 70, 91, 100%, baked in hot air oven.

There was little movement, so the 10 min. settling time is not anough.

posts.author: Dutchelm05
posts.content_md:
Getting there info

Still some whitening on the first plate. The drips are a little confusing if you are using the mold method. The second holo illuminated in green light I gather, hard to say if it has any whitening.

I would suggest the following:

See about using an established gelatin, that other DCG folks have tried (I am still willing to send you some Knox if you would like)

Consider light fixing as one of the forum members (Joe) uses. I believe he uses a 100 watt bulb although not sure of the time. Although I think it is great that you are try combinations of chemicals, I would recommend getting a good baseline established first. As I see it either you gelatin is too soft or your fixing is not adequate. By using a different fixing method, you might be able to islolate the problem. As all DCG'ers know, variables are abundant and interacting and is easy to achieve good results one day then crap the next.

Consider using a dull coin on the corner of your shots. Place the plate right on top of the coin. After processing, see what kind of level of "burn in" you have. If the coin image is deeply etched on to the plate, then you are most likely over exposed, if it is very dim, then you may be under exposed. 

Thanks for sharing with us, it is particularly great for me since I am not the resident rookie anymore 

Keep at it!

In the experiments, what I made before without adding TMG to adjust th pH, but with the same mix 100/12/4 i put the gelatine rigth on the big padlock, what I use as the test object. ![holo2.jpg](https://holographyforum.org/forum/download/file.php?id=6183)

The strange dips on the plate may be the dust. There are also the little channels, which arise when I separate the sanwich. Some parts of gelatine still stick together, bud another are seperated like the drains of water runs. It is like separating normally glued glass. I do not know, how to improve this step. 

My gelatine is the cooking pork type, bloom about 250, 220 minimum. I use ammonium dichromate p.a. grade and distilled water. Today I going to try one plate, which a leaved from the same batch, so the plate is 2 days old.

posts.author: info.crew
posts.content_md:
> what was different?If it is age of the film then of coarse your gel was too soft which makes sense right?I'm not a gelatin expert maybe John can comment on this.Can you explain your process from when you place the mold on top of the emulsion to how it drys?It could be a drying process issue.

I am not sure about the difference. Day before I exposed 10 and 25 minutes and last the time was 20 and 40 minutes. So the age affects the milkyness - probably the overtall hardening. 

I use the follows mold process: wash the mold glass (common mirror) with WC cleaner, rinse it well, treat it with rain x (similar product which I get here), polish it well with cloth. Then I put the plates and the mirror into the hot air oven cca 50°C. After that I place the mirror on leveled surface, pour with gelatine and place the plate on in. I take in this step just one plate from the oven to get same temp. after puting 4 plates i leave it cca 30 min to thicken it and then i put it to the fridge for cca 1 hour. After separating the sandwich I place it oliquely across the wall. Usually I use the fan to dry it quickly to prevent re-melting the gelatine in this hot days.

posts.author: dave battin
posts.content_md:
> **info.crew:** After separating the sandwich I place it oliquely across the wall. Usually I use the fan to dry it quickly to prevent re-melting the gelatine in this hot days.

After you separate the mold the gelatin still has all the h20 in it, you now must allow it to dry on a fairly level surface and allow it to dry with no heat, as this would cause your gelatin to liquefy again .......

posts.author: Dutchelm05
posts.content_md:
Dave is correct on this info. I have not coated anything this week since the weather is so hot.

So as you said about the big differences is the age of the film and the exposure. These both add to the hardness. I think the photo shows you are a bit over exposed (green in color) but you must expose more in order to prevent whitening. I think it is pretty clear that you have the following options:

Less exposure time, more fixer time

Add light fixing (i.e 100 watt bulb) after the exposure and you can still fix if you want, this will harden your film without effecting the image 

A better gelatin

Best of luck and hope to see more in the future.

Tony
